column1: A Simple Model of Monetary Policy under Phillips-Curve Causal Disagreements

The thesis A Simple Model of Monetary Policy under Phillips-Curve Causal Disagreements by Ran Spiegler explores a static textbook model of monetary policy  challenging the conventional assumption that the private sector has rational expectations. Instead  it posits that the private sector forms inflation forecasts based on a misspecified subjective model that disagrees with the central bank's true model regarding the causal underpinnings of the Phillips Curve. The private sector's model is represented using a directed acyclic graph (DAG)  a concept borrowed from the AI/Statistics literature on Bayesian Networks. This approach allows for the examination of how the private sector's incorrect causal model can lead to rigid inflation forecasts  resulting in an attenuation effect in the central bank's optimal policy  which is sensitive to the noisiness of the true inflation-output equations.

The thesis begins by discussing the importance of expectations management in monetary policy  as highlighted by Woodford (2003)  and critiques the conventional assumption of model communism  where the private sector shares the central bank's model of the macroeconomy. Spiegler relaxes this assumption by allowing the private sector to form its forecasts based on a different model  particularly focusing on the causal interpretation of the Phillips Curve. The paper draws on historical debates in macroeconomic thought  which have often revolved around disagreements over causality in the Phillips Curve.

Spiegler adopts the formalism of Bayesian networks to model the private sector's causal understanding  using a DAG to represent economic variables and their causal influences. This model is fitted to the steady-state distribution  and the private sector uses it to produce inflation forecasts. When the model is misspecified  these forecasts systematically distort the true expected inflation  affecting the central bank's policy decisions.

The central bank's objective is to minimize a quadratic loss function of the deviations of output and inflation from their targets. The analysis reveals two key insights: first  the private sector's incorrect causal model can lead to rigid inflation forecasts  causing the central bank's response to the inflation target to be weaker than in the rational-expectations benchmark. Second  the variance of noise terms in the inflation-output equations plays a crucial role in this effect  especially when the private sector's model reverses the direction of causality between inflation and output.

The thesis also addresses the ambiguity in the macroeconomic literature regarding the flatness of the Phillips relation  distinguishing between a weak yet precise relation and a noisy relation. In the rational-expectations framework  the variance of noise terms is irrelevant for the private sector's forecast and the central bank's policy. However  with a misspecified model  the variance of noise terms subtly affects the private sector's inflation forecast and  consequently  the central bank's policy.

Overall  Spiegler's work provides a nuanced understanding of how disagreements over the causal structure of the Phillips Curve can impact monetary policy  highlighting the importance of considering the private sector's potentially flawed causal models in policy design.
